learn.title: Renewable Purchase Obligation in India Explained
learn.intro: The Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) compels DISCOMs to buy a fixed share of their power from renewables. It is India's main regulatory lever to push utilities away from coal and accelerate the clean energy transition at grid scale.
learn.c1_text: RPO is a legal mandate requiring distribution companies to procure a minimum percentage of their total electricity from renewable sources. Think of it as a healthy diet prescription: just as doctors require food companies to meet nutrition standards, regulators force DISCOMs to source green power.
learn.c2_text: DISCOMs can meet RPO targets either by buying renewable power directly via PPAs or by purchasing Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) on power exchanges. Each REC represents 1 MWh of clean electricity, giving utilities a flexible, market-based pathway to compliance.
learn.c3_text: India's RPO trajectory has risen from 5% in 2012 to roughly 22.5% by 2025, with sub-targets for solar and wind. CERC and state electricity regulators enforce compliance through penalties, shaping how DISCOMs plan their long-term power procurement portfolios.
learn.stat1: India RPO target: 22.5% of total consumption by FY 2025
learn.stat4: Over 75 DISCOMs across India are bound by RPO

learn.title: Rooftop Solar and Net Metering in India
learn.intro: Rooftop solar lets homes and businesses generate their own electricity using panels mounted on roofs. Combined with India's net metering policy, it turns every rooftop into a mini power plant, slashing bills and feeding surplus energy back to the grid.
learn.c1_text: Solar panels on your roof convert sunlight into DC electricity using the photovoltaic effect. An inverter then converts this DC into AC power that runs your lights, fans, and appliances. On sunny days, a 3 kW system can generate around 12-15 units daily.
learn.c2_text: A bidirectional net meter tracks both energy you draw from the grid and surplus you export. Your bill reflects the net difference. Imagine a seesaw: daytime exports offset nighttime imports, and unused credits often roll forward for up to a billing cycle.
learn.c3_text: India's PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana aims to solarize 10 million households with 300 units of free electricity monthly. The scheme provides ₹78,000 subsidy per household and has re-energized rooftop adoption after several states moved toward net-billing.
learn.stat1: India rooftop solar target: 40 GW by 2026
learn.stat2: Subsidy: up to ₹78,000 per household under PMSGY
learn.stat4: A 3 kW system typically costs ₹1.95 lakh after subsidy

learn.title: Perovskite Solar Cells: Beyond Silicon
learn.intro: Perovskite solar cells are a next-generation photovoltaic technology that promise high efficiency at low cost. Unlike rigid silicon, they can be printed as thin films, opening possibilities for lightweight, flexible, and even transparent solar surfaces.
learn.c1_text: Perovskites are a class of materials with a specific crystal structure, often hybrid organic-inorganic lead halides. They absorb sunlight extremely well, so a film just 0.5 micrometers thick can generate as much current as a 200-micrometer silicon wafer.
learn.c2_text: In lab conditions, single-junction perovskite cells have reached over 26% efficiency, rivaling mature silicon. Tandem stacks pairing perovskite with silicon have crossed 33%, suggesting a clear roadmap to push past silicon's theoretical ceiling of about 29%.
learn.c3_text: Perovskites degrade when exposed to moisture, heat, and UV light, typically lasting far less than silicon's 25-year lifespan. Researchers are testing encapsulation, 2D perovskite layers, and tin-based variants to improve durability for commercial deployment.
learn.stat3: Perovskite cell thickness: ~0.5 μm vs 200 μm for silicon
learn.stat4: Global perovskite R&D investment exceeded $1 billion by 2024

learn.title: Building Integrated Photovoltaics: Solar as Architecture
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics, or BIPV, replace conventional building materials like roof tiles, facade panels, and windows with solar-generating materials. It turns the entire building envelope into a power plant, blending clean energy generation with modern architecture.
learn.c1_text: BIPV products are photovoltaic materials that serve dual roles: generating electricity AND acting as structural or weatherproof building elements. Examples include solar roof shingles, curtain wall spandrels, semi-transparent skylights, and facade cladding that doubles as a power source.
learn.c2_text: Traditional rooftop arrays are bolted onto existing structures, requiring extra mounting and leaving the old roof in place. BIPV replaces the building material itself, eliminating redundant layers, reducing material costs, and improving aesthetics for premium real estate.
learn.c3_text: India's ECBC (Energy Conservation Building Code) and net-zero building push are opening doors for BIPV. Projects in Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Delhi-NCR are piloting solar facades and BIPV canopies, especially for commercial complexes aiming for LEED-India Platinum ratings.
learn.stat1: Global BIPV market projected: $86 billion by 2032
learn.stat3: BIPV can reduce building energy use by 30-50%
learn.stat4: India commercial building floor area: ~1.2 billion sq ft eligible for BIPV
learn.readLabel: Read at US Dept of Energy

learn.title: Hydrogen Colour Code: Blue, Green, and Grey Explained
learn.intro: Not all hydrogen is created equal. The industry uses a colour-coded system to distinguish how hydrogen is produced, because the source of energy and the resulting emissions dramatically change its role in climate goals. Blue, green, and grey are the most discussed today.
learn.c1_text: Grey hydrogen is produced from natural gas via steam methane reforming (SMR) without capturing the CO2 released. It is the cheapest and most common form today, accounting for about 95% of global hydrogen, but emits around 9-10 kg of CO2 for every kg of hydrogen made.
learn.c2_text: Blue hydrogen uses the same SMR process as grey, but captures and stores up to 90-95% of the CO2 emissions underground via CCS. Think of it as grey hydrogen wearing a carbon-filter mask. It is seen as a bridge fuel while green hydrogen infrastructure scales up globally.
learn.c3_text: Green hydrogen is made by electrolysing water using electricity from renewable sources like solar and wind. Zero emissions at the point of production. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen production by 2030, backed by ₹17,000 crore in funding.
learn.stat1: Grey hydrogen share: ~95% of global production
learn.stat2: Green H2 target India: 5 MMT by 2030
learn.stat3: SMR emissions: ~9-10 kg CO2 per kg H2
learn.stat4: Blue H2 capture rate: 90-95% via CCS

learn.title: Agrivoltaics: Farming and Solar on the Same Land
learn.intro: Agrivoltaics is the practice of co-locating solar panels and crops on the same piece of land. It offers a clever solution to the food-versus-energy debate, letting farmers harvest both sunshine and crops from a single field, while increasing total land productivity.
learn.c1_text: Solar panels are mounted higher than usual, around 2-3 meters above ground, with wider spacing between rows. This allows tractors, livestock, and sunlight to pass underneath. Think of it as installing a solar parasol over the field, providing partial shade that certain crops love.
learn.c2_text: Panels reduce heat stress on plants by lowering ground temperature by 2-4°C, decreasing water evaporation by up to 30%. Shade-tolerant crops like tomatoes, spinach, and berries often thrive, while the panels themselves produce clean electricity, doubling farmer income streams.
learn.c3_text: India has piloted agrivoltaic projects in states like Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Rajasthan. The ICAR-Central Arid Zone Research Institute has shown successful cultivation of cotton and turmeric under elevated solar arrays, with yields comparable to open-field farming plus solar revenue.
learn.stat1: Land productivity boost: up to 60-70% in agrivoltaic setups
learn.stat2: Water savings for crops: 20-30% under PV shade
learn.stat4: India's solar-agro target under PM-KUSUM covers 15 lakh farmers
